title: A Resilient Water System
premise: Help a remote community design a reliable, low-maintenance water system before the next dry season.
impact: A practical solution here could provide clean water, stronger food production, and greater independence for the community.

chapters.title: Is the spring enough?
chapters.scene: The village sits below a spring that has never run dry, but in the dry season its flow drops to its lowest. Before anyone digs a trench, the council asks the first question: will it be enough? At the end of the last dry season, a villager timed how long the spring took to fill a 20-liter bucket.
givens: A 20-liter bucket filled in 250 seconds, with the spring at its lowest.
chapters.question: How many liters does the spring give in a full day at its lowest?
chapters.method: 20 liters in 250 seconds is 0.08 liters a second. 0.08 × 60 × 60 × 24 = 6,912 liters a day.

right.text: 6,912 liters a day. Two hundred people at about 20 liters each need about 4,000 liters a day, so the spring is enough, with room to spare. The council lets out a breath.

wrong.text: The council won't commit to a number nobody can explain. Someone climbs back up to time the bucket again: five days lost.

data: About 200 people live in the village.
Basic access to water is usually reckoned at about 20 liters per person per day: enough for drinking, cooking and basic washing, not much more.

chapters.title: The drop
chapters.scene: The spring is 45 meters higher than the lowest point of the pipe, where it reaches the village. With no pumps, that height is what moves the water. Before choosing a pipe, you need to know how hard the water will push on it there when every valve is closed and the water stands still.
givens: Height of the spring above the lowest point of the pipe: 45 meters
chapters.question: What pressure, in kilopascals, will the still water put on the pipe at its lowest point?
chapters.method: Pressure = density × gravity × height = 1,000 × 9.81 × 45 = 441,450 pascals: about 441 kPa, or 4.4 bar. Every 10 meters of height adds about 1 bar.

right.text: About 441 kPa, or 4.4 bar. Whatever pipe runs along the lowest stretch has to hold that, with a margin to spare.

wrong.text: Your number goes into the report as it is. It will matter when you choose the pipe.

data: The pipe runs 1.2 km from the spring, downhill nearly all the way; its lowest point is where it reaches the village.
1 bar is 100 kPa.
In still water, pressure depends on the height of water above a point, not on the pipe's length or width.

chapters.title: Choosing the pipe
chapters.scene: Three suppliers have quoted for 1.2 km of pipe, and a retired engineer from the next valley has a fourth idea. Whatever you choose has to be carried up the mountain path, laid in a trench, and hold up at the bottom for years with almost no maintenance.

options.label: Plastic pipe (HDPE), rated PN4
options.detail: Light coils, quick to lay. $9,000, about 35 days to install.
options.outcome: The coils go up the path quickly. Printed on every meter: PN4.

options.label: Plastic pipe (HDPE), rated PN6
options.detail: Light coils, quick to lay. $12,000, about 35 days to install.
options.outcome: The coils go up the path quickly. Printed on every meter: PN6, a comfortable margin over the 4.4 bar at the bottom.

options.label: PN4 pipe, with a small open tank halfway down
options.detail: The engineer's idea: a little concrete tank, open to the air, with a float valve, halfway down the drop. $9,000 of pipe and $1,500 for the tank, about 38 days.
options.outcome: Halfway down, the water spills into the little tank and starts again from there. No stretch of pipe now holds more than about 22 meters of water above it, about 2.2 bar, well within PN4.

options.label: Galvanized steel pipe
options.detail: Very strong, but heavy, in 6-meter lengths joined by hand, and it rusts where its coating is damaged. $26,000, about 60 days to install.
options.outcome: It will hold any pressure here, but every length has to be carried up and threaded by hand, and it leaves little money for anything else.

chapters.explain: Tell the council why you chose it.
rubric: compares each pipe's rating with the pressure at the bottom (about 4.4 bar)
leaves a margin for the surges when taps close
weighs the cost against a budget that must also build a tank and tap stands
considers carrying, laying and looking after it in a remote place
data: PN ratings give the pressure, in bar, a plastic pipe is made to carry continuously (at 20 °C).
Closing a tap quickly sends a pressure surge back up the pipe, above the still-water pressure.
The engineer says the little tank would let the water start again halfway down.
Each quote is for pipe wide enough to carry the spring's steady flow.
HDPE pipe is light and flexible, comes in long coils, and lasts for decades buried.
The budget also has to pay for a storage tank, four tap stands, fittings and labor.

chapters.title: The morning rush
chapters.scene: The design is taking shape when a grandmother at the council asks what everyone in the village already knows: nobody draws water at midnight. In the morning, before work and school, everyone comes at once.
givens: Between 6 and 8 in the morning, the village draws about 1,800 liters.
The spring gives 0.08 liters a second, day and night.
chapters.question: If the taps were fed straight from the spring, with no tank, how many of those 1,800 liters would be missing by 8 o'clock?
chapters.method: In two hours the spring gives 0.08 × 60 × 60 × 2 = 576 liters. 1,800 − 576 = 1,224 liters short.

right.text: About 1,224 liters short, every morning. The spring gives plenty in a day, but not enough at once. Water that runs all night into a tank can cover the rush.

wrong.text: Without the number, the council argues for a week about whether a tank is worth the money. Seven days lost.

data: Water use follows the day: a rush in the morning, a smaller one in the evening, little at night.
The spring's flow doesn't change through the day.

chapters.title: Where the water waits
chapters.scene: The council agrees to a tank of about 6,000 liters: enough for the morning rush, and a day's water if the pipe ever needs repair. Three places are offered for it.

options.label: On the knoll above the village
options.detail: Ten meters above the highest tap. The long pipe fills it day and night; short pipes run down from it to the taps.
options.outcome: The tank sits ten meters above the taps: enough height to push the water out, and close enough that the short pipes to the taps can carry the whole morning rush.

options.label: Beside the spring
options.detail: Easy to build on solid rock at the top. The long pipe would then carry the water from the tank down to the village.
options.outcome: The tank fills beside the spring, but now the whole morning rush has to come down 1.2 km of pipe at once, and the pipe was chosen for the spring's steady flow. A wider pipe costs another $4,000 and five days.

options.label: In the village square, beside the taps
options.detail: Easy to reach and to keep an eye on. It sits at the same level as the taps.
options.outcome: Everyone can see the tank from the square, and the long pipe fills it through the night.

rubric: the tank has to sit higher than the taps, so gravity can push the water out
keeps the long pipe carrying a steady flow, with the tank covering the rush
considers building and looking after the tank
considers keeping the stored water clean
data: Water flows out of a tank by gravity only as far as it has height to fall.
The long pipe was chosen to carry the spring's steady flow, not the morning rush.
Ferrocement tanks are built on site from cement, sand and wire mesh.

chapters.title: An unexpected expense

event.text: The cement supplier writes: prices are up 25%. The tank you planned for $8,000 will now cost $10,000.

chapters.scene: Share out what you can afford. Whatever you don't spend now stays in hand for surprises, and there are always surprises.

buckets.label: The 6,000-liter tank
buckets.short: A smaller tank: the morning rush drains it, and there's no day in reserve if the pipe breaks.

buckets.label: Four tap stands ($1,500 each)
buckets.short: Fewer tap stands: longer walks and longer queues.

buckets.label: Fittings and labor
buckets.short: Too few hands: the work goes slower, about 15 days more.

chapters.explain: What did you fund in full, what did you cut, and what did you keep back?
rubric: fits the total within the budget left
funds a tank big enough to cover the rush
keeps some money back for surprises
explains any cut, and why it does the least harm
data: Whatever isn't spent now stays in the budget for later.
With four tap stands, each serves about 50 people.
A day's water for 200 people at 20 liters each is 4,000 liters.

chapters.title: The pressure test

event.text: At the pressure test, the gauge at the bottom of the line reads 4.4 bar. The pipe is printed PN4. The supplier's engineer won't sign it off.

chapters.scene: A pipe that runs above its rating every day, with a surge each time a tap snaps shut, is a pipe that splits. The trench at the bottom is still open. There's still time to fix it.

options.label: Replace the lowest 400 meters with PN6 pipe
options.outcome: The bottom stretch, where the pressure is highest, is now PN6. The test passes.

options.label: Add a small open tank halfway down
options.detail: A little concrete tank, open to the air, with a float valve. $1,500 and about 6 days.
options.outcome: Halfway down, the water starts again from the open tank; below it, the pressure tops out around 2.2 bar. The test passes, on the pipe you already laid.

options.label: Run it anyway
options.detail: It's only 0.4 bar over. Nothing to pay, no days lost.
options.outcome: The engineer writes his objection in the logbook, and the trench is closed.

chapters.explain: Tell the engineer what you've decided, and why.
rubric: recognizes the pipe would run above its rating
fixes the stretch where the pressure is highest
compares the fixes on cost and time
considers surges, not just the still-water pressure
data: The pressure is highest at the bottom of the line and falls going up.
The lowest 400 meters of the line drop about 10 meters.
An open tank halfway down would split the 45-meter drop in two.

chapters.title: The approaching storm

event.text: A storm is forecast in three days. The trench across the steep slope above the village is half dug, and the village is running low on supplies.

chapters.scene: Rain on an open trench can wash the slope, and the pipe in it, away. But every day you wait is a day closer to the dry season, and families are already rationing water.

options.label: Keep working through the storm
options.detail: No time lost now, but an open trench on a steep slope in heavy rain.
options.outcome: The rain comes harder than forecast. Part of the slope slides into the trench, and a section of pipe has to be dug out and laid again: twelve days.

options.label: Stop and secure the site
options.detail: Cover the trench, anchor the pipe, bring the crew down. About 7 days lost.
options.outcome: The storm passes over a covered trench. A week lost, nothing broken.

options.label: Reroute along the hillside below the slope
options.detail: A longer, safer line that stays below the spring all the way: 300 meters more pipe ($3,000) and about 10 days.
options.outcome: The longer line costs more, but it no longer crosses the slope that slides.

options.label: Cut over the ridge
options.detail: The shortest way, and well away from the slope: the ridge path climbs about 10 meters above the spring. About 4 days, and no new pipe.
options.outcome: The first water stops at the foot of the ridge. Water moving by gravity can't climb higher than where it started. The crew digs the line up again and lays it around the shoulder of the hill: nearly four weeks, in the end.

chapters.explain: Tell the crew what you've decided, and why.
rubric: weighs the crew's safety
weighs the risk to the pipe against the days lost
checks that any new route stays below the spring
considers the days left before the dry season
data: Landslides are most likely on steep slopes with loose, wet soil.
The crew is ten volunteers from the village.
The spring is the highest point the water starts from.

chapters.title: Who keeps it running?
chapters.scene: Water runs at the taps. Before the team leaves, the council asks the question every water system faces: when a valve leaks or a pipe cracks next year, who fixes it, and with what money?

options.label: Train two caretakers, and start a repair fund
options.detail: Tools and spare parts left with them, and a small monthly fee from each family, agreed at a village meeting. $800 and about 4 days.
options.outcome: Two caretakers learn to cut and join pipe, clean the tanks and flush the line. The first month's fees go into a tin box at the council house.

options.label: Leave it to the district water office
options.detail: They'll send a technician when something breaks. Nothing to pay now.
options.outcome: The district thanks you. It has one technician for forty villages.

options.label: Hand it over and go
options.detail: The village built it; the village will manage.
options.outcome: A celebration in the square, and the team drives away.

chapters.explain: Tell the council how the system will keep running.
rubric: someone in the village is responsible for repairs
money is set aside before something breaks
spare parts and tools are on hand
the village agrees to it, not just the team
data: Studies find about one in four village handpumps in sub-Saharan Africa out of order at any one time.
Plastic pipe can be cut and joined with simple tools and fittings.
A leak or a blocked tank left alone for weeks can leave the whole village without water.

endings.title: A split at the bottom
endings.text: Water reaches the village on the first day. Three months later, on a morning when the taps snap shut one after another and surge after surge runs up the line, the pipe splits at its lowest stretch, where it had been running above its rating. The council finds the money to replace it, but the village carries water through the first weeks of the dry season. It's a lesson every water engineer learns early: rate the pipe for its lowest point, with a margin.

endings.title: Not before the dry season
endings.text: The work runs past the first dry weeks. The system is finished and it works, but the village carried water for a while yet. Days were the scarcest thing you had.

endings.title: Water at a trickle
endings.text: The tank fills every night, and every morning the taps barely run: the tank sits at their level, with no height left to push the water out. The next year the village moves the tank up to the knoll. Water needs somewhere to fall.

endings.title: It worked, for a while
endings.text: Water runs at all four tap stands before the dry season. Eighteen months later, a valve starts leaking at the tank, and no one is sure whose job it is. By the time it's fixed, the village has carried water for weeks. A water system lasts as long as someone looks after it.

endings.title: Water, with strain
endings.text: Water runs at the taps before the dry season. Something you couldn't afford, or a setback you couldn't avoid, will be felt: longer queues, less water in store, or less time to spare. A working system, with less margin than the village hoped for.

endings.title: Water before the dry season
endings.text: Water runs at all four tap stands weeks before the dry season: from a pipe that never holds more than it's rated for, a tank above the village that the night fills and the morning empties, and two caretakers with a tin box of savings. Two hundred people stop carrying water up the hill.
